background: In September 2024, the French national pension fund Assurance Retraite suffered a data breach affecting approximately 370k assistance beneficiaries . The data included 70k unique email addresses along with names, dates of birth, physical addresses, phone numbers, income levels, marital statuses, French social security numbers (NIR) and contact details of relatives or other nominated contacts. In its disclosure notice, Assurance Retraite attributed the breach to a compromised partner account .
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: 70,372 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Dates of birth, Email addresses, Family members' names, Government issued IDs, Income levels, Marital statuses, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses.
editorial: The people in this set were assistance beneficiaries of France's national pension fund, and the record makes their circumstances plain: income levels and marital statuses sit alongside names, addresses, phone numbers and French social security numbers (NIR). It is hard to design a better list for fraud aimed at vulnerable people. The field that stands out is the contact details of relatives or other nominated contacts.

That turns one person's record into a small family tree, and it enables the scam where a caller claims to be from the pension fund, already knows the beneficiary's details, and asks a son or daughter to help "update the file" or pay a fee to keep the benefit. The cause, a compromised partner account, is also typical.

Large public bodies increasingly share data with service partners, and the partner is often the weaker link. If you or a relative receive support from l'Assurance retraite, treat any call asking for bank details or a fee as fraud. Hang up and call back on the number from an official letter you already have. The dates add a further warning.
The breach occurred in September 2024 and HIBP added the data in October 2026, two years later, and the record counts about 370,000 affected beneficiaries but only 70,000 unique email addresses.

Many of the people in the dataset are older and may not use email at all, which means the follow-up fraud is more likely to arrive by phone or post than by phishing link, and the HIBP count understates how many households are exposed.

A French social security number cannot be changed, and combined with a date of birth and address it supports attempts to open accounts or claim benefits in someone else's name. Relatives who help an older parent manage their paperwork are in a good position to watch for this: unexpected letters from banks, mobile providers or benefits offices are the early sign.
The guide to spotting phishing covers the email side; for phone and post, the rule is the same as above: hang up, and call back on a number you already hold.

fields.name: Government issued IDs
fields.why: Passport and licence numbers are used to prove identity to banks and telecoms, and they are effectively permanent.

fields.name: Physical addresses
fields.why: Where someone actually lives. Combined with a name this moves the risk off the internet.

fields.name: Phone numbers
fields.why: Enables SIM-swap attacks against SMS two-factor codes, and puts the number on scam-call lists indefinitely.

fields.name: Dates of birth
fields.why: One of the three things call centres ask to verify identity, and it never changes.

fields.name: Names
fields.why: Turns an anonymous address into an identified person, which is what makes targeted phishing possible.

fields.name: Email addresses
fields.why: An exposed address may be used in phishing attempts. Treat unexpected messages with caution.

fields.name: Family members' names
fields.why: Adds detail to a profile that can be assembled from several breaches at once.

fields.name: Income levels
fields.why: Adds detail to a profile that can be assembled from several breaches at once.

fields.name: Marital statuses
fields.why: Adds detail to a profile that can be assembled from several breaches at once.

actions: Move two-factor authentication off SMS and onto an authenticator app, which a SIM swap cannot intercept.
Consider a credit freeze. A government identifier cannot be changed, so limiting what can be opened in your name is the only real control.
Be sceptical of post and callers who already know your address, knowing it is no longer evidence of anything.
Be alert to phishing. A message may use details from exposed or collected records to appear familiar; verify requests through the service directly.
